title: Dispersion — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Dispersion's rich face: two made walks, one that shows what wave dispersion is from a single wave up to the test that one bend of one curve decides both of its signatures, and one that builds the page's all-pass recipe and puts it to the page's first open question; beside them, the pieces three neighbours made this round where this hub's sentences are exactly what they test. I grow when the entry is enriched again, next toward the loudspeaker and granular meanings, which have nothing made yet; I never hold the entry's words.

pieces.file: Dispersion — rich — what spreads, and which way.html
pieces.title: what spreads, and which way · five steps
pieces.caption: **Does the section's “sharp (or flat)” name a free choice, or one fact?** One wave on a plain string, its crest at one speed whatever the wavelength; the same wavelength on a plain, a stiff and a beaded string, three crest speeds; two waves making a swell that runs at its own speed, faster than its crests on the stiff string and slower on the beaded one (heard as a beat that quickens or slows); a pulse that keeps its shape, sheds ripples ahead, or sheds them behind, with each string's curve of frequency against wavelength; and last the test. Between two ends the stiff string's partial 16 sits 196 cents sharp and the beaded string's 181 flat; down a long string the stiff one lands 1.2 kHz 31 ms before 250 Hz and the beaded one 250 Hz 43 ms before 1.2 kHz. Sharp comes with highs first and flat with lows first, as any curve that bends one way all along requires; a curve with a bend both ways could split them, and none is shown here. The numbers are measured from the engine's own renders of each law, so they check the code; what the step tests is whether the two signatures, read off one curve two ways, agree. Not heard by the agent that made it.

pieces.file: /Projects/Piano String Inharmonicity/Piano String Inharmonicity — rich — stretch.html
pieces.by: Piano String Inharmonicity's maker, this round
pieces.title: where the partials go · Piano String Inharmonicity
pieces.caption: **The section's own formula, walked.** This page writes the stiff string's partials as n·f0·√(1 + B·n²); Piano String Inharmonicity's face walks exactly that: one partial, which barely moves (f0 is the stiffness-free pitch, not the one you hear), the row of twelve against its ghosts, one partial beating against its ghost, and last the cube law of the stretch, which holds while B·n² is small and gives way toward a square past n ≈ 1/√B.

pieces.title: the law against the rule · Particle Synthesis, 2026-10-22
pieces.caption: **The spread let out by physics, and the same spread mapped by a rule.** 22,666 strikes from one set of throws. A: each strike travels the fountain's ice by the plate's law, and the spectrogram is a weather of slanted chirps. B: each strike fires a decaying sine whose pitch is chosen by distance, the usual granular mapping, and the picture is one band sliding down. Set beside the section's sentence that in particle synthesis the spread falls out of the physics: this sets physics against a mapping, not against random spread, and says nothing yet about gravity converging or drag scattering.

pieces.caption: 1024 particles, the spread made by the throws and carried to the pickups by the ice's law. Loudness matched to B.

pieces.caption: The same throws and strikes, pitch set by distance, 2 kHz near to 200 Hz far. Whether A reads as physics and B as a mapping is an ear's call; nobody had listened when these were made.

pieces.file: /Projects/Particle Synthesis/Particle Synthesis — rich — which way the colours run.html
pieces.title: which way the colours run · Particle Synthesis
pieces.caption: **The prism's two facets, tested on real glass.** White light through Schott N-BK7: violet turned most, red least, as this section says. The same glass as a kilometre-long road, a flash travelling at the group index: red arrives first and violet last, red 656 nm ahead of blue 486 nm by 76 ns. Then a click through the fountain's ice (highs first) and the deep-water law (lows first), on one table. It tests this section's temporal facet, and finds the glass slows the shorter wavelengths, not the longer ones.
pieces.near: Temporally, wavelengths travel at different phase velocities

pieces.title: the recipe, built · five steps
pieces.caption: **Does the recipe buy a dispersive medium, and can you tell its copy from the string?** One first-order all-pass (level one everywhere; the lows held back; its zero outside the unit circle, so not minimum-phase, and still causal); the same section many times in a row, a click opening into a falling chirp; a cascade fitted to a click's twelve trips along a stiff string (B = 0.001, f0 = 110 Hz: 512 sections and a 489-sample delay line, within 0.23 ms of the string's delay from 80 Hz to 10 kHz, the chirp's bands landing within 0.15 ms); a struck harmonic note through that cascade, whose partials stay on the harmonic grid (within 0.002 cents) while the stiff string's go sharp (partial 16, 196 cents); and last a blind pair at four stiffnesses, the string against the copy, loudness matched. The recipe buys the chirp's timing and not the stretch. Whether the pair can be told apart at B = 0.0001, where partial 16 is 22 cents sharp, is left to the ear: no agent has heard it.

pieces.file: /Dispersion Table/Dispersion Table — rich — the warp knob.html
pieces.title: the warp knob · Dispersion Table
pieces.caption: **The same cascade put inside the loop.** One second-order all-pass, eight in log steps, the eight inside a Karplus-Strong string, and a pole radius swept from pure through piano to an irregular end. Where the walk above leaves a struck note's partials on the grid, this one moves them, because the delay is paid again on every trip: the place the recipe needs to be to make a stretch, not only a chirp.

offers.what: 'The audible signature is inharmonicity — upper partials drift sharp (or flat)' holds between two ends, and the 'or' is not free. The piece reads one curve two ways. Stiff string (B = 0.001, f0 = 110 Hz): partials 8 and 16 sit +52.8 and +196.4 cents from n × the first, and down a long string (250 ms for long waves) 1.2 kHz lands 31.4 ms before 250 Hz. Beaded string (31 beads): −44.0 and −181.1 cents, and 250 Hz lands 42.7 ms before 1.2 kHz. Plain: neither. Sharp comes with highs first and flat with lows first for any law that bends one way all along, since a curve from zero that bends up both steepens (the group speed rises) and steepens its line from zero (the phase speed rises). In open travel the same curve's signature is a chirp, not inharmonicity. Suggested, after 'the bell-like ring of a tense piano string': 'Between two ends the signature is inharmonicity; in open travel it is a chirp; and the two go together: a law that bends up (stiff strings and bars) sends partials sharp and highs first, one that bends down (a beaded string, a lattice, deep water) sends them flat and lows first.'

'It arises wherever a restoring force couples nonlinearly to inertia' reads as nonlinearity, and the three strings in the piece are all linear: what bends the curve is a restoring force that depends on wavelength (bending stiffness adds a term in k⁴; the beads' spacing caps the frequency; gravity on deep water gives ω = √(g·k)). Piano String Inharmonicity's offer on its LTI section makes the same point. From physics, not from the piece: 'room modes' is not an example of frequency-dependent propagation speed, since air carries every audio frequency at one speed and a room's modes come from its walls. Suggested: 'It arises wherever the restoring force depends on wavelength: stiff strings and bars, lattices, waveguides whose cross-section matters, deep-water waves.'

The formula pairs an angular frequency with a frequency in hertz: 'ω_n = n f0 √(1 + B n²)'. The piece reads it as f_n = n·f0·√(1 + B·n²) (exact: the stiff law read at ν = n·f0 matches it to 2e-16), with f0 the stiffness-free fundamental, 0.87 cents below the first partial at B = 0.001 (Piano String Inharmonicity's offer says the same). Suggested: 'f_n = n·f0·√(1 + B·n²) (B = stiffness coefficient, f0 the fundamental the string would have with no stiffness)'.

'Temporally, wavelengths travel at different phase velocities through the glass (longer paths delay longer wavelengths)' runs the wrong way for glass. Particle Synthesis's gathered piece, on Schott's N-BK7 index: the shorter wavelengths are slowed more; over 1 km, red 656 nm leads blue 486 nm by 76.0 ns, and red 700 nm leads violet 410 nm by 161 ns. A pulse's colours separate by group velocity, not phase velocity. Suggested: 'Temporally, a flash's colours travel at different speeds through the glass, and the shorter wavelengths are slowed more, so violet arrives last.'

Three of the section's conditions are off, as the piece's first step shows. (1) 'minimum-phase': an all-pass section is not minimum-phase. Its zero sits at radius 1 ⁄ |a| outside the unit circle (1.111 at a = −0.9), and a minimum-phase filter with level one everywhere is a plain wire: its phase is fixed by its magnitude, so it cannot delay one frequency more than another. (2) 'maximum-phase IRs violate causality': the all-pass numerator a + z⁻¹ is maximum-phase, two taps, and causal; its first sample comes at once. What violates causality is an anticausal response. (3) 'positive and nonlinear in ω': a delay that is a straight line in ω still spreads a click. With τ = β·ω, 30 ms more at 8 kHz, bands land at 0.98, 3.89, 15.0 and 29.6 ms for 250 Hz, 1, 4 and 8 kHz, a 28.6 ms rising chirp (the check; the deep-water law is this case, as Particle Synthesis's colours piece hears it). It is the phase that must be nonlinear; the delay need only vary. Suggested: 'if the impulse response is all-pass (level one everywhere, so not minimum-phase) and its group delay τ(ω) = −dφ/dω varies with ω.' Drop the maximum-phase clause.

The recipe buys the chirp of one fixed passage, not a dispersive resonator's inharmonicity. Fitted to a click's twelve trips along a stiff string (B = 0.001, f0 = 110 Hz), 512 first-order sections and a 489-sample delay line match the string's delay within 0.225 ms from 80 Hz to 10 kHz, and the chirp's bands land within 0.15 ms (0.30 at 125 Hz). But a struck harmonic note convolved with that cascade keeps every partial on n·f1 (within 0.0012 cents), while the stiff string's partial 16 is 196.4 cents sharp. A time-invariant filter cannot move a frequency. The stretch comes from convolving with the medium's whole response (a struck string is exactly that) or from the cascade inside a feedback loop, where the delay is paid on every trip (Dispersion Table's warp knob). The cost is not small: 1024 multiplies a sample at B = 0.001 and 2688 at B = 0.0001. Suggested, after 'without simulating the full physics': 'Fed forward, it gives a click the medium's chirp but leaves a held tone's partials where they were; to stretch them, put the cascade inside the loop.'

Question 1 is partly answered, and the rest is a listening test now on the face. If the crafted IR is the medium's whole response, convolution is the medium: a struck string is that convolution (Piano String Inharmonicity's click piece agrees with it to −228 dB). If it is the all-pass recipe fed a harmonic source, the difference is the stretch: partial 16 sits +606.9, +196.4, +63.8 and +21.8 cents from n × the first at B = 0.004, 0.001, 0.0003 and 0.0001 in the string and 0.0 in the copy, while the chirp's timing matches within 0.23 ms. Whether a listener hears the difference at small B is untested; the blind pair in 'the recipe, built' is there for it. Suggested: add one line under question 1 naming the two cases, and leave the threshold open.
